claim: Serum Kallistatin levels are significantly elevated in AD patients compared to normal controls (12.78 ± 2.80 μg/ml vs 9.78 ± 1.93 μg/ml).
source: In addition, the serum Kallistatin (12.78 ± 2.80 μg/ml) content in patients with AD was greater than that in normal controls (9.78 ± 1.93 μg/ml) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements from 56 AD patients and 61 healthy controls, with statistical significance shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Fasting blood glucose and triglyceride levels are greater in AD patients than in healthy controls.
source: Similarly, fasting blood glucose and triglyceride (TG) levels were greater in AD patients than in healthy controls (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by clinical measurements from patient cohorts, with data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Kallistatin and TG contents are further elevated in AD patients with diabetes compared to AD patients without diabetes (13.79 ± 3.05 μg/ml).
source: Further according to diabetes status, all the AD patients were grouped and found that the Kallistatin (13.79 ± 3.05 μg/ml) and TG contents were further elevated in AD patients with diabetes (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by subgroup analysis of AD patients stratified by diabetes status, with data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Kallistatin expression is increased in the hippocampus of AD model mouse SAMP8 compared to control mouse SAMR1.
source: Similarly, Kallistatin expression was increased in the hippocampus of the AD model mouse SAMP8 compared with that in the control mouse SAMR1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of hippocampal tissue from SAMP8 and SAMR1 mice, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The Kallistatin concentration is increased in metabolic abnormality-related AD patients.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the Kallistatin concentration is increased in metabolic abnormality-related AD patients.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing elevated Kallistatin in AD patients with hyperglycemia and hypertriglyceridemia.

claim: KAL-TG mice exhibit longer escape latency times in the Morris water maze test compared to age-matched WT mice.
source: Notably, the latency to escape the platform was longer, and the number of platform crossings, percentage of time spent, and spontaneous alternation were significantly lower in KAL-TG mice than in age-matched WT mice (Figure 1E–I).
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing data from Morris water maze experiments across multiple age groups (3, 6, 9, and 12 months), shown in Figure 1E-I.

claim: KAL-TG mice show significantly lower number of platform crossings, percentage of time spent in target area, and spontaneous alternation compared to WT mice.
source: Notably, the latency to escape the platform was longer, and the number of platform crossings, percentage of time spent, and spontaneous alternation were significantly lower in KAL-TG mice than in age-matched WT mice (Figure 1E–I).
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing data from Morris water maze and Y-maze tests, shown in Figure 1E-I.

claim: Long-term potentiation (LTP) in hippocampal CA1 neurons is significantly reduced in KAL-TG mice compared to WT mice.
source: The LTP in KAL-TG mice was significantly reduced compared to that in WT mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings of CA1 neurons in acute hippocampal slices from KAL-TG and WT mice at 3, 6, and 12 months, shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Kallistatin impairs cognitive memory in mice.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that Kallistatin could impair cognitive memory in mice.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral and electrophysiological data showing cognitive deficits in KAL-TG mice.

claim: Plaque density in KAL-TG mice is much greater than in age-matched WT mice.
source: Predictably, the plaque density and tau phosphorylation in KAL-TG mice were much greater than those in age-matched WT mice (Figures 2A–C–3A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and western blot analysis of hippocampal tissues, shown in Figures 2A-C and 3A-D.

claim: Tau phosphorylation in KAL-TG mice is much greater than in age-matched WT mice.
source: Predictably, the plaque density and tau phosphorylation in KAL-TG mice were much greater than those in age-matched WT mice (Figures 2A–C–3A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and western blot analysis showing increased phosphorylated tau (p-tau S396, p-tau T231, and p-tau S202) in hippocampal tissues, shown in Figures 3A-D.

claim: Aβ42 content in hippocampal tissue is extraordinarily increased in KAL-TG mice compared with WT mice.
source: Consistent with these results, ELISA detection of the Aβ42 content in hippocampal tissue revealed that Aβ production was extraordinarily increased in KAL-TG mice compared with WT mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of Aβ42 in hippocampal tissue from KAL-TG and WT mice, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Kallistatin promotes Aβ deposition and tau phosphorylation.
source: These results suggested that Kallistatin promoted Aβ deposition and tau phosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from in vivo data showing increased Aβ plaques and tau phosphorylation in KAL-TG mice.

claim: Aβ levels in primary hippocampal neurons infected with Kallistatin adenovirus are greater than in control groups.
source: Western blot and ELISA analyses revealed that the Aβ levels in primary hippocampal neurons (immunofluorescence identified with the neural marker MAP2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) infected with the Kallistatin adenovirus were greater than those in the control groups (Figure 2E–G), as were those in the HT22 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by western blot and ELISA measurements from primary hippocampal neurons infected with Kallistatin adenovirus, shown in Figures 2E-G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aβ levels in HT22 cells infected with Kallistatin adenovirus are greater than in control groups.
source: Western blot and ELISA analyses revealed that the Aβ levels in primary hippocampal neurons (immunofluorescence identified with the neural marker MAP2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) infected with the Kallistatin adenovirus were greater than those in the control groups (Figure 2E–G), as were those in the HT22 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by western blot and ELISA measurements from HT22 cells infected with Kallistatin adenovirus, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: BACE1 protein and mRNA levels are greater in the hippocampus of KAL-TG mice compared to WT mice.
source: Compared with those in WT mice, BACE1 protein and mRNA levels were greater in the hippocampus of KAL-TG mice (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), whereas no significant difference in APP, PS1, or α-secretase (Adam9, Adam10, or Adam17) expression was detected (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot, immunohistochemistry, and RT-qPCR analysis of hippocampal tissue from KAL-TG and WT mice, shown in Figures 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant difference in APP, PS1, or α-secretase (Adam9, Adam10, or Adam17) expression is detected between KAL-TG and WT mice.
source: Compared with those in WT mice, BACE1 protein and mRNA levels were greater in the hippocampus of KAL-TG mice (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), whereas no significant difference in APP, PS1, or α-secretase (Adam9, Adam10, or Adam17) expression was detected (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot and RT-qPCR analysis showing no significant changes in these proteins, shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BACE1 activity is increased in KAL-TG mice compared to WT mice.
source: Consistent with the above results, the activity of BACE1 increased (Figure 4D), whereas PS1 activity did not change (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of β-secretase activity in hippocampal tissue, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PS1 activity does not change in KAL-TG mice compared to WT mice.
source: Consistent with the above results, the activity of BACE1 increased (Figure 4D), whereas PS1 activity did not change (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements of γ-secretase activity in hippocampal tissue, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: BACE1 expression and activity are increased in primary mouse neurons and HT22 cells transfected with Kallistatin adenovirus.
source: Similarly, the expression and activity of BACE1 were found to be increased in primary mouse neurons and HT22 cells transfected with Kallistatin adenovirus (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), while PS1 expression and activity remained unchanged (Figure 5A, D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blot and ELISA measurements from primary neurons and HT22 cells, shown in Figures 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: PS1 expression and activity remain unchanged in primary mouse neurons and HT22 cells transfected with Kallistatin adenovirus.
source: Similarly, the expression and activity of BACE1 were found to be increased in primary mouse neurons and HT22 cells transfected with Kallistatin adenovirus (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), while PS1 expression and activity remained unchanged (Figure 5A, D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blot and ELISA measurements showing no change in PS1, shown in Figures 5A, D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The effect of Kallistatin on Aβ production is attenuated by BACE1 inhibitor verubecestat.
source: Additionally, the effect of Kallistatin was attenuated by the BACE1 inhibitor verubecestat or siBace1 03, which was the most effective (Figure 5E, F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing reduced Aβ and BACE1 levels when verubecestat is used with Kallistatin overexpression, shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The effect of Kallistatin on Aβ production is attenuated by siBace1 03.
source: Additionally, the effect of Kallistatin was attenuated by the BACE1 inhibitor verubecestat or siBace1 03, which was the most effective (Figure 5E, F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing reduced Aβ and BACE1 levels when siBace1 03 is used with Kallistatin overexpression, shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Kallistatin can promote Aβ generation through the upregulation of BACE1 expression.
source: These results indicate that Kallistatin can promote Aβ generation through the upregulation of BACE1 expression.
evidence: Inferred from data showing increased BACE1 expression and activity with Kallistatin overexpression, and attenuation by BACE1 inhibition.

claim: PPARγ is decreased in the hippocampal tissue of KAL-TG mice.
source: PPARγ decreased in the hippocampal tissue of KAL-TG mice, as detected by western blot and immunohistochemical analysis (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunohistochemistry analysis of hippocampal tissue, shown in Figures 5G-J.

claim: No significant differences in YY1 or SP1 expression are detected in KAL-TG mice compared to WT mice.
source: However, no significant differences in YY1 or SP1 expression were detected (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing no change in YY1 or SP1 protein levels, shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Kallistatin downregulates the expression of PPARγ in primary hippocampal neurons and HT22 cells, thus increasing BACE1 and Aβ expression.
source: In addition, Kallistatin downregulated the expression of PPARγ in primary hippocampal neurons and HT22 cells, thus increasing BACE1 and Aβ expression (Figure 5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of primary neurons and HT22 cells infected with Kallistatin adenovirus, shown in Figure 5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Treatment with rosiglitazone, a PPARγ agonist, reverses the decrease in PPARγ caused by Kallistatin.
source: Treatment with rosiglitazone, a PPARγ agonist, reversed the decrease in PPARγ caused by Kallistatin (Figure 5K, L).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing restoration of PPARγ levels with rosiglitazone treatment, shown in Figures 5K, L.

claim: Rosiglitazone inhibits the ability of Kallistatin to promote BACE1 and Aβ.
source: Predictably, rosiglitazone inhibited the ability of Kallistatin to promote BACE1 and Aβ (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing reduced BACE1 and Aβ levels with rosiglitazone treatment in Kallistatin-overexpressing cells, shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Notch1 is highly expressed in the hippocampal tissues of KAL-TG mice.
source: Quantitative assessments in mice models indicated that Notch1 was highly expressed in the hippocampal tissues of KAL-TG mice (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunohistochemistry analysis of hippocampal tissue from KAL-TG and WT mice, shown in Figures 6A-D.

claim: Notch1 expression is upregulated in primary hippocampal neurons and HT22 cells infected with adenovirus expressing Kallistatin.
source: Furthermore, Notch1 expression was upregulated in primary hippocampal neurons and HT22 cells infected with adenovirus expressing Kallistatin in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of primary neurons and HT22 cells, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Kallistatin can directly bind to the Notch1 receptor and activate the Notch1 pathway.
source: Additionally, Kallistatin could directly bind to the Notch1 receptor and activate the Notch1 pathway (Figure 6E, F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by Co-IP analysis and membrane extraction experiments showing direct binding between Kallistatin and Notch1, shown in Figures 6E, F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Treatment with siNotch1 03 to knock down Notch1 inhibits the effect of Kallistatin on the activation of the Notch1 signaling pathway.
source: Treatment with siNotch1 03, which was the most effective (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), to knock down Notch1 inhibited the effect of Kallistatin on the activation of the Notch1 signaling pathway, leading to the downregulation of HES1, upregulation of PPARγ, and downregulation of BACE1 and Aβ (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing changes in Notch1 pathway components when Notch1 is knocked down, shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Hes1 shRNA 1 upregulates PPARγ and decreases the production of BACE1 and Aβ when neurons are infected with adenovirus to overexpress Kallistatin.
source: Similarly, Hes1 shRNA 1, the most effective (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), upregulated PPARγ and decreased the production of BACE1 and Aβ when neurons were infected with adenovirus to overexpress Kallistatin (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing changes in PPARγ, BACE1, and Aβ levels when HES1 is knocked down, shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Kallistatin promotes Aβ production via direct binding to the Notch1 receptor and activating the Notch1 pathway.
source: These results suggest that Kallistatin promotes Aβ production via direct binding to the Notch1 receptor and activating the Notch1 pathway.
evidence: Inferred from data showing direct binding of Kallistatin to Notch1, activation of Notch1 signaling, and downstream effects on BACE1 and Aβ production.

claim: GSK-3β is activated in the hippocampus of KAL-TG mice.
source: Consistent with previous reports, western analysis in both in both in vivo and in vitro models demonstrated that GSK-3β was activated in the hippocampus of KAL-TG mice (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing decreased p-GSK-3β (Ser9) levels in hippocampal tissue, indicating GSK-3β activation, shown in Figures 7A, B.

claim: An increase in tau phosphorylation is observed with the activation of GSK-3β induced by Kallistatin overexpression.
source: Moreover, an increase in tau phosphorylation was observed with the activation of GSK-3β induced by Kallistatin overexpression (Figure 7C, D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which was reversed by LiCl, an inhibitor of GSK-3β (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis of primary neurons and HT22 cells showing increased p-tau levels with Kallistatin overexpression, shown in Figures 7C, D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LiCl, an inhibitor of GSK-3β, reverses the increase in tau phosphorylation induced by Kallistatin overexpression.
source: Moreover, an increase in tau phosphorylation was observed with the activation of GSK-3β induced by Kallistatin overexpression (Figure 7C, D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which was reversed by LiCl, an inhibitor of GSK-3β (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis showing reduced p-tau levels when LiCl is used with Kallistatin overexpression, shown in Figures 7E, F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Kallistatin promotes tau phosphorylation by activating the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: These findings confirmed that Kallistatin promoted tau phosphorylation by activating the Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: Inferred from data showing GSK-3β activation and increased tau phosphorylation with Kallistatin overexpression, and reversal by GSK-3β inhibition.

claim: The behavioral performance of fenofibrate-treated KAL-TG mice is improved compared to untreated KAL-TG mice.
source: Compared with that of the KAL-TG group, the behavioral performance of the treated group was improved, as measured by the MWM and Y-maze tests.
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing data from Morris water maze and Y-maze tests comparing fenofibrate-treated and untreated KAL-TG mice.

claim: The latency to reach the escape platform on the fifth training day is significantly decreased in the fenofibrate-treated group compared to the rosiglitazone-treated group.
source: The latency to reach the escape platform on the fifth training day was significantly decreased (Figure 8B), and the number of platform crossings (Figure 8C), percentage of time spent (Figure 8D), and spontaneous alternation (Figure 8F) were significantly greater in the fenofibrate-treated group than in the rosiglitazone-treated group.
evidence: Supported by Morris water maze test data comparing fenofibrate and rosiglitazone treatment groups, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The number of platform crossings, percentage of time spent, and spontaneous alternation are significantly greater in the fenofibrate-treated group than in the rosiglitazone-treated group.
source: The latency to reach the escape platform on the fifth training day was significantly decreased (Figure 8B), and the number of platform crossings (Figure 8C), percentage of time spent (Figure 8D), and spontaneous alternation (Figure 8F) were significantly greater in the fenofibrate-treated group than in the rosiglitazone-treated group.
evidence: Supported by Morris water maze and Y-maze test data, shown in Figures 8C, D, F.

claim: Decreased serum Kallistatin levels, Aβ and BACE1 levels, phosphorylation of tau, and activation of GSK3β are detected in the fenofibrate-treated KAL-TG group.
source: In addition, decreased serum Kallistatin levels, Aβ and BACE1 levels, phosphorylation of tau, and activation of GSK3β were detected in the fenofibrate-treated KAL-TG group (Figure 8G–K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA and western blot analysis of serum and hippocampal tissue from fenofibrate-treated KAL-TG mice, shown in Figures 8G-K.

claim: There is no significant difference between the rosiglitazone-treated group and the KAL-TG group in terms of serum Kallistatin levels, Aβ and BACE1 levels, phosphorylation of tau, and activation of GSK3β.
source: However, there was no significant difference between the rosiglitazone-treated group and the KAL-TG group (Figure 8G–K).
evidence: Supported by ELISA and western blot analysis showing no significant changes in these parameters with rosiglitazone treatment, shown in Figures 8G-K.

claim: Kallistatin is a novel regulator of Aβ plaque accumulation, tau protein hyperphosphorylation, and metabolic abnormality-related cognitive memory impairment.
source: A molecular and biochemical approach demonstrated that Kallistatin is a novel regulator of Aβ plaque accumulation, tau protein hyperphosphorylation, and metabolic abnormality-related cognitive memory impairment.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive experimental data showing Kallistatin's effects on Aβ, tau, and cognitive function.

claim: Kallistatin transcriptionally upregulates Bace1 expression by suppressing the transcriptional repressor PPARγ, leading to Aβ cleavage and production.
source: Mechanistically, Kallistatin transcriptionally upregulates Bace1 expression by suppressing the transcriptional repressor PPARγ, leading to Aβ cleavage and production.
evidence: Supported by data showing decreased PPARγ and increased BACE1 expression with Kallistatin overexpression, and reversal by PPARγ agonist.

claim: Kallistatin can bind directly to the Notch1 receptor and activate the Notch1/HES1 pathway, causing a decrease in PPARγ, overproduction of BACE1, and increased Aβ42 generation.
source: Most importantly, the experimental findings revealed that Kallistatin could bind directly to the Notch1 receptor and activate the Notch1/HES1 pathway, causing a decrease in PPARγ, overproduction of BACE1, and increased Aβ42 generation.
evidence: Supported by Co-IP data showing direct binding, and western blot data showing pathway activation and downstream effects.

claim: Kallistatin can induce tau phosphorylation by activating GSK-3β, which results from the inhibition of LRP6.
source: Moreover, Kallistatin can induce tau phosphorylation by activating GSK-3β, which results from the inhibition of LRP6.
evidence: Inferred from data showing GSK-3β activation and increased tau phosphorylation with Kallistatin overexpression, combined with previous reports of Kallistatin as a Wnt inhibitor.

claim: Prolonged stimulation with high concentrations of Kallistatin impairs cognitive memory in mice.
source: Finally, prolonged stimulation with high concentrations of Kallistatin impaired cognitive memory in mice.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from KAL-TG mice showing cognitive deficits.

claim: The hypolipidemic drug fenofibrate decreases Aβ expression, tau phosphorylation, and serum Kallistatin level in KAL-TG mice, alleviating memory and cognitive impairment.
source: Finally, the hypolipidemic drug fenofibrate decreased Aβ expression, tau phosphorylation, and the serum Kallistatin level in KAL-TG mice, alleviating memory and cognitive impairment.
evidence: Supported by behavioral, ELISA, and western blot data from fenofibrate-treated KAL-TG mice.

claim: These observations establish an association between high Kallistatin levels and metabolic abnormality-related AD.
source: For the first time, these observations establish an association between high Kallistatin levels and metabolic abnormality-related AD and provide a new drug candidate (fenofibrate) for AD patients with metabolic syndromes.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive data showing elevated Kallistatin in AD patients with metabolic abnormalities and the mechanistic studies.

claim: Fenofibrate is a new drug candidate for AD patients with metabolic syndromes.
source: For the first time, these observations establish an association between high Kallistatin levels and metabolic abnormality-related AD and provide a new drug candidate (fenofibrate) for AD patients with metabolic syndromes.
evidence: Inferred from the therapeutic effects of fenofibrate in KAL-TG mice.

claim: About 80% of AD patients are insulin resistant or have T2DM.
source: About 80% of AD patients are insulin resistant or have T2DM de la Monte, 2014; additionally, T2DM patients have a higher risk of up to 73% dementia than healthy controls do (Koekkoek et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to de la Monte, 2014.

claim: T2DM patients have a higher risk of up to 73% dementia than healthy controls.
source: About 80% of AD patients are insulin resistant or have T2DM de la Monte, 2014; additionally, T2DM patients have a higher risk of up to 73% dementia than healthy controls do (Koekkoek et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koekkoek et al., 2015.

claim: The process of cognitive decline in T2DM patients appears to begin in the prediabetic phase of insulin resistance.
source: In line with these observations, the process of cognitive decline in T2DM patients appears to begin in the prediabetic phase of insulin resistance (Biessels and Reagan, 2015; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Biessels and Reagan, 2015 and Xu et al., 2010.

claim: GAD disease enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes in neurons of T2DM patients and normal controls reveals a close relationship between AD and T2DM.
source: A GAD disease enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes in the neurons of T2DM patients and normal controls revealed a close relationship between AD and T2DM.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis of gene expression data from GSE161355, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PFAM analysis identifies an enrichment of the Serpin family protein domain in differentially expressed genes between T2DM and normal neurons.
source: Additionally, PFAM analysis identified an enrichment of the Serpin family protein domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by PFAM analysis using the DAVID database, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Kallistatin (serpin family a member 4) is elevated in the serum of T2DM patients and is associated with an adverse prognosis of diabetes complications.
source: Kallistatin (serpin family a member 4) was elevated in the serum of T2DM patients and was associated with an adverse prognosis of diabetes complications (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2019.

claim: Kallistatin concentrations are significantly elevated in dementia patients compared to healthy control subjects.
source: Serum samples were collected from 11 dementia patients at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital, and Kallistatin concentrations were observed to be significantly elevated compared to those in healthy control subjects (Long et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Long et al., 2024.

claim: Nearly 95% of AD patients are categorized as sporadic patients, whose increasing incidence and mortality are strongly associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), obesity, and hyperlipidemia.
source: Nearly 95% of AD patients are categorized as sporadic patients, whose increasing incidence and mortality are strongly associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), obesity, and hyperlipidemia (Cardoso et al., 2017; Schipper, 2011; Folch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cardoso et al., 2017; Schipper, 2011; Folch et al., 2015.

claim: About 37% of comorbidities between AD and diabetes have been reported in the Alzheimer's Association Report.
source: About 37% of comorbidities between AD and diabetes have been reported in the Alzheimer's Association Report (Alzheimer's Association, 2016; Baglietto-Vargas et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alzheimer's Association, 2016 and Baglietto-Vargas et al., 2016.

claim: AD has been termed 'type 3 diabetes' by some researchers due to the strong association and shared mechanism between AD and T2DM.
source: As a result of the strong association and shared mechanism between AD and T2DM, AD has been termed 'type 3 diabetes' by some researchers (Kandimalla et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Steen et al., 2005; Candasamy et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kandimalla et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Steen et al., 2005; Candasamy et al., 2020.

claim: Diabetes confers a 1.6-fold increased risk of developing dementia.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that diabetes confers a 1.6-fold increased risk of developing dementia (Koekkoek et al., 2015; Hildreth et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koekkoek et al., 2015 and Hildreth et al., 2012.

claim: Central obesity and high body mass index during middle age are associated with about a 3.5-fold increased risk of dementia later in life.
source: Similarly, central obesity and high body mass index during middle age are associated with about a 3.5-fold increased risk of dementia later in life (Anjum et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anjum et al., 2018.

claim: Kallistatin is a serine proteinase inhibitor previously identified as a tissue kallikrein-binding protein.
source: Kallistatin is a serine proteinase inhibitor previously identified as a tissue kallikrein-binding protein (Ma et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2018.

claim: Kallistatin is produced predominantly in the liver and is widely expressed in body tissues, where it has antiangiogenic, antifibrotic, antioxidative stress, and antitumor effects.
source: It is produced predominantly in the liver and is widely expressed in body tissues, where it has antiangiogenic, antifibrotic, antioxidative stress, and antitumor effects (Yang et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2020 and Ma et al., 2017.

claim: Kallistatin was found to be increased in patients with obesity, prediabetes, and diabetes.
source: Furthermore, Kallistatin was found to be increased in patients with obesity, prediabetes, and diabetes (El-Asrar et al., 2015; Gateva et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to El-Asrar et al., 2015; Gateva et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2010.

claim: The concentration of Kallistatin is positively correlated with the triglyceride glucose index.
source: The concentration of Kallistatin was positively correlated with the triglyceride glucose index (Nowicki et al., 2021), which was proven to be an independent risk factor for dementia (Hong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nowicki et al., 2021.

claim: The triglyceride glucose index is an independent risk factor for dementia.
source: The concentration of Kallistatin was positively correlated with the triglyceride glucose index (Nowicki et al., 2021), which was proven to be an independent risk factor for dementia (Hong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2021.

claim: The concentration of serum Kallistatin in T2DM patients is significantly increased.
source: In addition, evidence from our previous study revealed that the concentration of serum Kallistatin in T2DM patients was significantly increased and further revealed that Kallistatin suppressed wound healing in T2DM patients by promoting local inflammation, which suggested that Kallistatin plays a critical role in the progression of T2DM (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2019.

claim: Kallistatin suppresses wound healing in T2DM patients by promoting local inflammation.
source: In addition, evidence from our previous study revealed that the concentration of serum Kallistatin in T2DM patients was significantly increased and further revealed that Kallistatin suppressed wound healing in T2DM patients by promoting local inflammation, which suggested that Kallistatin plays a critical role in the progression of T2DM (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2019.

claim: Kallistatin can cause memory and cognitive dysfunction by disrupting the glutamate–glutamine cycle.
source: Furthermore, it was revealed that Kallistatin can cause memory and cognitive dysfunction by disrupting the glutamate–glutamine cycle (Long et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Long et al., 2024.

claim: Accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides and hyperphosphorylated tau proteins in the hippocampus triggers cognitive memory decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) peptides and hyperphosphorylated tau proteins in the hippocampus triggers cognitive memory decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AD pathology.

claim: The incidence and mortality of sporadic AD are tightly associated with diabetes and hyperlipidemia.
source: The incidence and mortality of sporadic AD were tightly associated with diabetes and hyperlipidemia, while the exact linked molecular mechanism is uncertain.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, though the mechanism is uncertain.

claim: Kallistatin could directly bind to the Notch1 receptor and thereby upregulate BACE1 expression by inhibiting PPARγ signaling, resulting in Aβ cleavage and production.
source: Mechanistically, Kallistatin could directly bind to the Notch1 receptor and thereby upregulate BACE1 expression by inhibiting PPARγ signaling, resulting in Aβ cleavage and production.
evidence: Supported by Co-IP, western blot, and functional assays showing direct binding and downstream effects.

claim: Kallistatin could promote the phosphorylation of tau by activating GSK-3β.
source: Besides, Kallistatin could promote the phosphorylation of tau by activating GSK-3β.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing GSK-3β activation and increased tau phosphorylation.

claim: Fenofibrate could alleviate cognitive memory impairment by downregulating Aβ and tau phosphorylation of KAL-TG mice.
source: Fenofibrate, a hypolipidemic drug, could alleviate cognitive memory impairment by downregulating Aβ and tau phosphorylation of KAL-TG mice.
evidence: Supported by behavioral, ELISA, and western blot data from fenofibrate-treated KAL-TG mice.

claim: Fenofibrate might have the potential for treating metabolism-related AD.
source: Collectively, the experiments clarified a novel mechanism for Aβ accumulation and tau protein hyperphosphorylation regulation by Kallistatin, which might play a crucial role in linking metabolic syndromes and cognitive memory deterioration, and suggested that fenofibrate might have the potential for treating metabolism-related AD.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data from KAL-TG mice treated with fenofibrate.

claim: AD is marked by a gradual decline in cognitive memory.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most prevalent irreversible neurodegenerative disorder associated with dementia in elderly individuals, is marked by a gradual decline in cognitive memory.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD clinical presentation.

claim: AD is pathologically identified by the presence of extracellular amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs).
source: Pathologically, AD is identified by the presence of extracellular amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) (Grundke-Iqbal et al., 1986; Haass and Selkoe, 2007; Holtzman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grundke-Iqbal et al., 1986; Haass and Selkoe, 2007; Holtzman et al., 2011.

claim: The excessive production of Aβ disrupts normal cellular functions, leading to synaptic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, tau hyperphosphorylation, and neuroinflammation.
source: According to the Aβ cascade hypothesis, the excessive production of Aβ disrupts normal cellular functions, leading to synaptic dysfunction, neurodegeneration, tau hyperphosphorylation, and neuroinflammation, which ultimately result in memory impairment in individuals with AD and dementia (Leng and Edison, 2021; De Strooper and Karran, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leng and Edison, 2021 and De Strooper and Karran, 2016.

claim: Aβ peptides are derived from the sequential cleavage of amyloid precursor protein (APP) by β-secretase (BACE1) and γ-secretase.
source: Aβ peptides are derived from the sequential cleavage of amyloid precursor protein (APP) by β-secretase (β-site APP cleaving enzyme 1, BACE1) and γ-secretase, thus making this cleavage process significant in AD pathology (Tomita, 2014; LaFerla et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tomita, 2014 and LaFerla et al., 2007.

claim: BACE1 is considered a highly promising therapeutic target for AD.
source: BACE1 is considered a highly promising therapeutic target. Several potent BACE1 inhibitors have progressed to advanced stages in clinical trials, emphasizing the role of BACE1 in Aβ production (Das and Yan, 2019; Crunkhorn, 2017; Yan and Vassar, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Das and Yan, 2019; Crunkhorn, 2017; Yan and Vassar, 2014.

claim: Tau is a microtubule-associated protein that naturally occurs in axons and regulates microtubule dynamics and axonal transport.
source: Tau, a microtubule-associated protein, naturally occurs in axons and regulates microtubule dynamics and axonal transport (Wang and Mandelkow, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Mandelkow, 2016.

claim: In AD, tau undergoes a multistep transformation from a natively unfolded monomer to large aggregated forms, such as NFTs.
source: In AD, tau undergoes a multistep transformation from a natively unfolded monomer to large aggregated forms, such as NFTs, another defining feature of AD (Hausrat et al., 2022; Braak et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hausrat et al., 2022 and Braak et al., 1994.

claim: GSK3 is a key kinase involved in the initial steps of tau phosphorylation.
source: Glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3) is a key kinase involved in the initial steps of tau phosphorylation, with Wnt signaling being crucial in activating GSK-3β and GSK-3β-mediated tau phosphorylation (Boonen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boonen et al., 2009.

claim: Wnt signaling is crucial in activating GSK-3β and GSK-3β-mediated tau phosphorylation.
source: Glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3) is a key kinase involved in the initial steps of tau phosphorylation, with Wnt signaling being crucial in activating GSK-3β and GSK-3β-mediated tau phosphorylation (Boonen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boonen et al., 2009.

claim: When Wnt signaling is activated, the LRP6 PPPSPxS motif can directly interact with GSK-3β and phosphorylate it.
source: When Wnt signaling is activated, the LRP6 PPPSPxS motif can directly interact with GSK-3β and phosphorylate it (Piao et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piao et al., 2008.

claim: When Wnt signaling is inhibited, GSK-3β becomes activated and dephosphorylated, allowing nonphosphorylated GSK-3β to add phosphate groups to serine/threonine residues of tau.
source: Consequently, when Wnt signaling is inhibited, GSK-3β becomes activated and dephosphorylated, allowing nonphosphorylated GSK-3β to add phosphate groups to serine/threonine residues of tau (Boonen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boonen et al., 2009.

claim: Kallistatin has been reported as a competitive inhibitor of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway.
source: Kallistatin has already been reported as a competitive inhibitor of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2013.

claim: A Notch mutation was reported to cause AD-like pathology.
source: For example, a Notch mutation was reported to cause AD-like pathology (Thijs et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thijs et al., 2003.

claim: The level of Notch1 is increased in AD patients.
source: In addition, the level of Notch1 was found to be increased in AD patients (Brai et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brai et al., 2016.

claim: The Notch1/HES1 signaling pathway has been reported to suppress the expression of PPARγ.
source: In addition, the Notch1/HES1 signaling pathway has been reported to suppress the expression of PPARγ (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Kallistatin can activate Notch1 signaling.
source: The precious findings demonstrated that Kallistatin can activate Notch1 signaling (Feng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feng et al., 2019.

claim: Kallistatin is a new ligand of the Notch1 receptor.
source: Here, the findings revealed that Kallistatin could activate Notch1 by binding directly to it, indicating that Kallistatin is a new ligand of the Notch1 receptor.
evidence: Inferred from Co-IP and functional data showing direct binding and activation.

claim: Multiple Aβ-targeted therapies tested in phase III clinical trials have failed to slow cognitive decline, although they can effectively reduce the Aβ load.
source: Unfortunately, several Aβ-targeted therapies tested in phase III clinical trials have failed to slow cognitive decline, although they can effectively reduce the Aβ load (Salloway et al., 2014; Ostrowitzki et al., 2017; Honig et al., 2018; Henley et al., 2019; Egan et al., 2019; Panza et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple clinical trial reports.

claim: BACE1 inhibitors have not only failed to improve the cognitive function of AD patients but have also resulted in clinical deterioration and liver function impairment.
source: BACE1 inhibitors have not only failed to improve the cognitive function of AD patients but have also resulted in clinical deterioration and liver function impairment (Wessels et al., 2020; Novak et al., 2020; Timmers et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wessels et al., 2020; Novak et al., 2020; Timmers et al., 2018.

claim: The reduction in BACE1 activity could lead to the accumulation of full-length APP.
source: Two possible reasons for the failure of clinical trials with BACE1 inhibitors are: first, the reduction in BACE1 activity could lead to the accumulation of full-length APP Nigam et al., 2016; second, the size of the BACE1 active site is relatively large, and the use of a small molecule may not be sufficient to occupy the active site (Citron, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nigam et al., 2016.

claim: The size of the BACE1 active site is relatively large, and the use of a small molecule may not be sufficient to occupy the active site.
source: Two possible reasons for the failure of clinical trials with BACE1 inhibitors are: first, the reduction in BACE1 activity could lead to the accumulation of full-length APP Nigam et al., 2016; second, the size of the BACE1 active site is relatively large, and the use of a small molecule may not be sufficient to occupy the active site (Citron, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Citron, 2002.

claim: PPARγ is a ligand-activated transcription factor and a master modulator of glucose and lipid metabolism, organelle differentiation, and inflammation.
source: PPARγ is a ligand-activated transcription factor and a master modulator of glucose and lipid metabolism, organelle differentiation, and inflammation (Zhao et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2016 and Guo et al., 2017.

claim: PPARγ agonists (rosiglitazone) could rescue memory impairment of AD model mice.
source: Growing evidence revealed that PPARγ agonists (rosiglitazone) could rescue memory impairment of AD model mice (Toledo and Inestrosa, 2010; Escribano et al., 2010; O'Reilly and Lynch, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Toledo and Inestrosa, 2010; Escribano et al., 2010; O'Reilly and Lynch, 2012.

claim: It is controversial whether rosiglitazone has a protective effect on memory cognitive function in clinical trials.
source: In clinical trials, it is controversial whether rosiglitazone has a protective effect on memory cognitive function (Watson et al., 2005; Tzimopoulou et al., 2010; Harrington et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Watson et al., 2005; Tzimopoulou et al., 2010; Harrington et al., 2011.

claim: KAL-TG mice exhibit no significant alterations in memory or cognitive function following 1-month rosiglitazone administration despite downward trajectory in Aβ expression.
source: The experimental data revealed that while Aβ expression demonstrated a downward trajectory, KAL-TG mice exhibited no significant alterations in memory or cognitive function following 1-month rosiglitazone administration (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by behavioral and western blot data from rosiglitazone-treated KAL-TG mice, shown in Figure 8.

claim: The lack of cognitive improvement with rosiglitazone could potentially be attributed to insufficient therapeutic duration and persistent unmodified Kallistatin concentrations.
source: These observations could potentially be attributed to insufficient therapeutic duration and persistent unmodified Kallistatin concentrations.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of effect of rosiglitazone.

claim: Fenofibrate is a fibric acid derivative for clinically lowering blood lipids, mainly triglycerides.
source: Fenofibrate is a fibric acid derivative for clinically lowering blood lipids, mainly triglycerides (Keating and Croom, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Keating and Croom, 2007.

claim: Fenofibrate could prevent memory disturbances, maintain hippocampal neurogenesis, and protect against Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Studies showed that fenofibrate could prevent memory disturbances, maintain hippocampal neurogenesis, and protect against Parkinson's disease (PD) (Barbiero et al., 2014; Ouk et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barbiero et al., 2014 and Ouk et al., 2014.

claim: Fenofibrate has a neuroprotective effect on memory impairment induced by Aβ through targeting α- and β- secretase.
source: Specifically, fenofibrate has a neuroprotective effect on memory impairment induced by Aβ through targeting α- and β- secretase (Assaf et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Assaf et al., 2020.

claim: Fenofibrate could repair the disrupted glutamine–glutamate cycle by upregulating glutamine synthetase.
source: Recently, the evidence from our previous study proved that fenofibrate could repair the disrupted glutamine–glutamate cycle by upregulating glutamine synthetase, while there is currently no fenofibrate treatment of AD in clinical trials (Long et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Long et al., 2024.

claim: There is currently no fenofibrate treatment of AD in clinical trials.
source: Recently, the evidence from our previous study proved that fenofibrate could repair the disrupted glutamine–glutamate cycle by upregulating glutamine synthetase, while there is currently no fenofibrate treatment of AD in clinical trials (Long et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Long et al., 2024.

claim: Fenofibrate administration in patients with metabolic syndrome plays an early role in preventing and treating AD.
source: Therefore, fenofibrate administration in patients with metabolic syndrome plays an early role in preventing and treating AD.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data from KAL-TG mice.

claim: Elevated circulating Kallistatin levels in individuals with comorbid AD and diabetes mellitus suggest a potential compensatory mechanism within the neuroendocrine regulatory axis.
source: Collective evidence from this investigation indicates elevated circulating Kallistatin levels in individuals with comorbid AD and diabetes mellitus, suggesting a potential compensatory mechanism within the neuroendocrine regulatory axis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the elevated Kallistatin levels observed in AD patients with diabetes.

claim: Kallistatin positively regulates Aβ42 through Notch1/HES1/PPARγ/BACE1.
source: In addition, it is the first time that Kallistatin was discovered positively regulating Aβ42 through Notch1/HES1/PPARγ/BACE1 and increased phosphorylated tau through inhibition of the Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive mechanistic data from in vivo and in vitro experiments.

claim: Kallistatin increases phosphorylated tau through inhibition of the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: In addition, it is the first time that Kallistatin was discovered positively regulating Aβ42 through Notch1/HES1/PPARγ/BACE1 and increased phosphorylated tau through inhibition of the Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by data showing GSK-3β activation and increased tau phosphorylation with Kallistatin overexpression.

claim: Kallistatin might play a crucial role in linking diabetes and cognitive memory deterioration.
source: Kallistatin might play a crucial role in linking diabetes and cognitive memory deterioration.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive data showing elevated Kallistatin in metabolic disorders and its effects on AD pathology.

claim: Fenofibrate could decrease the serum Kallistatin level, BACE1, Aβ, and phosphorylated tau of KAL-TG mice, leading to alleviating memory and cognitive impairment.
source: Moreover, fenofibrate could decrease the serum Kallistatin level, BACE1, Aβ, and phosphorylated tau of KAL-TG mice, leading to alleviating memory and cognitive impairment.
evidence: Supported by ELISA, western blot, and behavioral data from fenofibrate-treated KAL-TG mice.
